title: U.S. v. Sherman Booth
scope: This is a criminal case in which defendant, Sherman Booth, is charged with "obstructing, resisting and opposing the execution of process, and aiding, abetting and assisting the escape of Joshua Glover" from the Milwaukee County, Wisconsin jail. Glover, an escaped enslaved person, was jailed when his enslaver Benjamin Garland came north and under the Fugitive Slave Act attempted to recover him.  Booth with other Wisconsin abolitionists surrounded the jail, broke down the door, and rescued Glover by allowing him to escape. Booth was found guilty and sentenced to serve one month in jail, and to pay the cost of prosecution and a fine of $1,000. Booth appealed to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, and they unanimously declared the Fugitive Slave Act unconstitutional. The U.S. Supreme Court overturned that decision. Yet the Wisconsin Supreme Court refused to file the U.S. Court's mandate upholding the Fugitive Slave Act. Booth served out his jail term, but spent 10 months imprisoned for failure to pay the fine and prosecution costs.  President James Buchanan pardoned Booth on March 2, 1861. This case file includes the Presidential pardon, indictment, affidavits, recognizances, bills of costs, warrants, motions, summons, and commissioner's warrants.

title: Ohio Project Reports
scope:
This series consists of reports about soil conservation projects on public and privately owned lands in four Ohio watersheds located within Soil Conservation Service districts. The four projects were Project OH-1, affecting the Salt Creek watershed near Zanesville; Project OH-2 in the Muddy Fork River watershed near Wooster; Project OH-3 on Indian Creek near Hamilton; and Project OH-4 on Granny-Dry Creek near North Vernon.

The reports include drawings, color-coded maps of soil conservation project areas, charts of statistics, and graphs. Each report also features numerous photographs of woods, creeks, farm fields, and gullies; rain gauges and a silt-measuring device; erosion-controlling features such as flumes, contoured furrows around hillocks, and small dams constructed of stones, logs, or woven wire; and crews of men constructing such devices.

title: Records of the Indianapolis Office
scope:
This series consists of the records of the Indianapolis District Office in the Price Department in Region III of the Office of Price Administration (OPA). Region III was headquartered in Cleveland and had jurisdiction over district and local price boards in Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, and West Virginia.

Cards Containing Data on Dry Groceries cover the years 1943-1945 and contain information in coded form on community wholesale and retail prices of chain stores for dry groceries. The key to the code is on the front card of each group.

Records Relating to Pricing Zones for Dry Groceries in Indiana cover 1942-1945 and included memoranda, maps of proposed community food pricing zones, and newspaper clippings documenting the history of pricing zones for dry groceries in Indiana.

Records Containing Economic Data covers 1945-1946 and  consists of records that were a byproduct of studies of the buildings and construction industry compiled in connection with the preparation and operation of area price orders and amendments. They include memoranda, letters, economic briefs, complete questionnaires, and tabulations, relating to surveys of prices of installed insulation, hard building materials, stock millwork, roofing and siding materials, plumbing, heating, and other commodities and services.

Docketed Case Files Relating to Building and Construction cover 1945-1946 and include orders, memoranda, correspondence, and financial papers relating to applications for price adjustment, petitions for amendments to regulations, and protests again price actions of the OPA.

Case Files Relating to the Maximum Average Price (MAP) Program cover 1945-1946. The maximum average price order (Supplementary Order 108) required clothing manufacturers to produce garments at prices similar to their 1943 average in order to restore production of low- and medium-priced goods. A typical company case file includes a quarterly report, a makeup report, MAP charts, and a copy of each order issued granting prices to new sellers, together with amendments, supplements, opinions, and memoranda relating to order.

title: The United States vs. Victor L. Berger, Adolph Germer, J. Louis Engdahl, William F. Kruse, and Irwin St. John Tucker
scope: This file consists of a criminal case in which the defendants Victor L. Berger, Adolph Germer, J. Louis Engdahl, William F. Kruse, and Irwin St. John Tucker were accused of violating the Espionage Act of 1917.  Berger was an Austrian–American socialist politician and journalist who was a founding member of the Social Democratic Party of America and served terms in Congress representing Wisconsin. Berger was convicted and sentenced to 20 years by Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis but the conviction was later overturned by the Supreme Court.
notes: While indicted, Berger was elected to the House of Representatives, but was unable to take his seat based on the decision of a Congressional special committee. Their decision included the following statement -  "In regard to the first question, your committee concurs with the opinion of the special committee appointed under House resolution No. 6, that Victor L. Berger, the contestee, because of his disloyalty, is not entitled to the seat to which he was elected, but that in accordance with the unbroken precedents of the House, he should be excluded from membership; and further, that having previously taken an oath as a Member of Congress to support the Constitution of the United States, and having subsequently given aid and comfort to the enemies of the United States during the World War, he is absolutely ineligible to membership in the House of Representatives under section 3 of the fourteenth amendment to the Constitution of the United States."

title: The United States of America v. Eugene V. Debs
scope: This is the criminal case file in the Eugene V. Debs sedition case. The file includes an indictment, appearances, bench warrants, exhibits, mandates, motions, petitions, photographs, orders, speeches, statement of proceedings, subpoenas, testimony, and a verdict.
notes: Debs, a leading member of the Socialist Party, gave an anti-war speech on June 16, 1918 in Canton, Ohio.  He was later indicted on June 29, 1918 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern (Cleveland) Division of the Northern District of Ohio for violating the Espionage Act of 1917.  Debs was convicted by a jury on September 12, 1918, and sentenced to federal prison.  He appealed the ruling to the Supreme Court of the United States.  On April 12, 1919, the Supreme Court confirmed the courts verdict and Debs was sentenced to 10 years imprisonment.  In December 1921, President Warren G. Harding commuted Debs' sentence to time served and he was released.

title: Records Related to Legal Precedents
scope:
This series consists of records relating to criminal and civil investigations and prosecutions in southern Ohio by the office of the United States Attorney for the Southern Judicial District of Ohio.  This district has offices in Columbus, Cincinnati, and Dayton.  The files may include correspondence, notes, memoranda, copies of court documents, transcripts of testimony, exhibits, printed material, Federal Bureau of Investigation reports, telegrams, photographs, and news clippings.

title: Records Relating to Legal Precedents
scope:
This series consists of selected case files from the Office of the U.S. Attorney for the Northern Judicial District of Illinois. The cases documented in these files were considered to be either historically significant or important factors in setting legal precedents. They refer primarily to governmental investigations of criminal and civil violations of various Federal statutes that occurred within the Northern District of Illinois. The District encompasses Lake, Kane, DuPage, Cook, Kendall, Will, La Salle, Grundy, JoDaviess, Stephenson, Winnebago, Boone, McHenry, Carroll, Ogle, DeKalb, Whiteside, and Lee counties in Illinois.

Among the more notable case files are those relating to the prosecution of Alphonse Capone and Moses Annenberg for income tax evasion, Hans Haupt for treason in World War Two, the German American Bund for violating the Voorhis Act, Illinois Governor Otto Kerner Jr. for bribery, and the Chicago Seven (Eight) for conspiracy to incite a riot.  The files also include numerous examples of less well known Federal prosecutions involving efforts to avoid the draft, auto theft, impersonating a member of the military, forgery, fraud, mail theft and abuse of the mail, interstate travel of stolen goods, illicit drug sales, extortion, corruption, illegal gun sales, pollution, and other crimes.

The Chicago Seven (Eight) trial covers the prosecution of David T. Dellinger of the National Mobilization Committee to End the War in Vietnam, Abby Hoffman and Jerry Rubin of the Youth International Party, Bobby Seale of the Black Panthers, and four others for conspiracy and inciting a riot following the 1968 Democratic Convention riots in Chicago.

The files contain numerous records that were used in the course of legal proceedings against the various defendants. These include legal correspondence, memorandums, photographs and other graphic material, depositions, subpoenas, financial records, criminal court records, evidence, and exhibits. Many case files contain reports compiled by agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and transcripts of grand jury testimony. Some audio and video recordings exist in this series, but the inventories are unable to identify which cases have recordings and which do not.

title: Republic Steel Corporation and Berger Manufacturing Company vs. Zurich General Accident and Liability Insurance Company, Limited

title: The United States of America vs. John Mohammad Ali
scope: This file consists of an suit brought by the United States for the cancellation of a certificate of citizenship for John Mohammad Ali, who was born in India. The petition alleges that the Ali received a certificate of citizenship on May 26, 1921 from the US District Court in Detroit and that at the time when said certificate was so issued said defendant was not a "free white person" nor a "person of African nativity or descent"; and that, therefore, he was not eligible for citizenship per section 15 of the Naturalization Act. This lawsuit followed the Supreme Court decision in United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind, in which the court ruled that people from India were "not white" and therefore ineligible for citizenship.

title: United States of America vs. Kurt von Reiswitz, Gustave H. Jacobsen, Albert H. Wehde, George Paul Boehm, Heramba Lal Gupta, Jodh Singh, Jnanendra Nath Sanyal, Chandra Kanta Chakraberty, otherwise called Chandra Kanta Chakrabarty, and one Scholtz, otherwise called Sterneck
scope: In Chicago, Gustav H. Jacobson, Albert H. Wehde, Heramba Lal Gupta, and George Paul Boehm were convicted under the Neutrality Act of 1794 for setting out on a military enterprise against the British Empire in India, and for conspiracy under Section 37 of the criminal code.  The lawyers for the defense agreed that the defendants had provided support for Indian nationalists, but argued that the Indian nationalists merely intended to bring about a revolution by means of political agitation, and disagreed with the broad definition of military enterprise used in the case.  The trial was held after the US entered World War 1, but the acts of conspiracy with German agents were committed prior to US entry into the war, and were therefore violations of neutrality laws.  One of the witnesses in the Chicago trial, Jodh Singh, was supplied by the British and was previously a witness in the Lahore Conspiracy trial, where participants in the Ghadar movement were executed for treason.  Gustav H. Jacobson was later pardoned by Calvin Coolidge.  This indictment was combined with Criminal Case 6082, so see NAID 540240450 for later records.
notes:
This case was part of a series of trials against persons of Indian descent affiliated with the Ghadar movement, which supported the overthrow of the British colonial government in India, and persons of German descent accused of conspiring with them to undermine Britain.  The cases are often called the Indo-German Trials, Hindu-German Conspiracy or Hindu Conspiracy, although Sikhs and Muslims were also involved.  Some of those indicted in the Chicago case were later tried in San Francisco instead.  The US prosecutors worked with British intelligence agents, who aided the case with significant evidence.  In addition to accepting support and money from German consulates, the Ghadar movement also had ties with the Irish Independence movement, and some of its members were socialists or anarchists. | See also

Marshall, Michigan resident Charles T. Gorham led a group of townspeople that prevented agents for Giltner in their attempt to return the fugitive enslaved persons to bondage. scope:
This file consists of an equity case that involved The Natural Food Company, of Niagara Falls, New York, against Henry P. Bulkley, of 75 West Van Buren Street, Chicago for taking and reproducing the 1893 patent of Henry D. Perky for a “new and useful improvement in bread,” a shredded wheat biscuit, which consisted of “bread composed of superposed deposits of dry, externally rough, porous, sinuous threads or filaments of cooked whole wheat, and free from leavening or raising material.” Henry D. Perky owned the Cereal Machine Company and introduced his invention at the 1893 Columbian Exposition, the Chicago World’s Fair. 

For his defense, Bulkley argued that “a biscuit is altogether outside of the range of design patents. A biscuit is made to be eaten, not to be admired by the eye.” 

The case documents include briefs, patents, bills, affidavits, decrees, motions, testimonies, and arguments.

title: John Herbert Dillinger Case File
scope:
This file consists of records created by the United States Attorney, Northern District of Indiana, Hammond, relating to John Herbert Dillinger. The records primarily document Dillinger's March 3, 1934 escape from Sheriff Lillian Holley's jail in Crown Point, Indiana. Dillinger used a fake handgun carved from wood to deceive guards. He was accompanied in the escape by another inmate, Herbert Youngblood. The records also document the Crown Point police Ford V-8 automobile theft by Dillinger and Youngblood during the escape. Included are transcripts of interviews with eyewitnesses and jail staff who were coerced into aiding Dillinger's escape. Transcripts of interviews with Ernest Blunk, Ralph Wright, Malcolm Fhech, Winfred Bryant, John Kowaliszyn, Edwin Saager, Sam Cahoon, Lewis Baker, Jimmy Posey, Fred Beaver, Henry Jeliaek, Lestser Carron, Matt Brown, Marshall Keithley, and Philip Schreiber are included in the records. 

The case file also documents the Dillinger gang's June 30, 1934 bank robbery of the Merchants National Bank in South Bend, Indiana. South Bend Patrolman Howard C. Wagner was killed in the robbery.

The case file includes a small number of late 20th-century and early 21st-century newspaper articles that describe Dillinger-related anniversaries and events in northern Indiana.

At issue were lands along the lakefront of Lake Michigan in the Chicago area that were reserved for the tribes in the Treaty of 1783 (The Treaty of Paris) and August 3, 1795 (Treaty of Greenville) and the Treaty of St Louis of August 24, 1816, which together granted "one piece of land six miles square at the mouth of Chicago River." Based on the government survey of 1821, named the Walls Survey, the plaintiffs claimed ownership of this land and demanded damages of fifty million dollars. 

The file includes affidavits, motions, stipulations, orders, and a pamphlet named "The Greatest Conspiracy Ever Conceived." Documents also list hundreds of members of the Ottawa, Chippewa, and Potawatomi tribes.

title: The President and Fellows of Harvard College vs. John B. Jewett, William F. Jewett, Madge R. Robbins, Charles E. Jewett, Ida S. Mathis, and Louisa E. Jewett
scope: This case file consists of a land dispute over ownership of a Native American burial site in Cincinnati, near what was known as Madisonville, Ohio before it was annexed. Referred to throughout as the "ancient Indian village and burial site", the land was owned by a Phebe Ferris, who allowed a local amateur anthropologist, Dr. C. L. Metz to excavate it in 1879. His findings led to the interest of the Peabody Museum, which is associated with Harvard University. Artifacts were shown at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and also wound up in the permanent holdings of the Peabody. In 1896, Phebe Ferris willed the land and any artifacts to the Peabody Museum. By 1911, the Peabody completed their excavations and removed ". . . skeletons, artifacts, and relics . . . ." and attempted to sell the land. At this point, the Ferris relatives filed suit to revert the ownership of the land back to the family since the Peabody and Harvard were no longer interested in ownership. The case was decided in favor of the heirs, but was subsequently appealed to the Sixth Circuit Court, Cincinnati.

scope: This file consists of an insurance dispute by the aunt of a United States Marine killed in World War I. title: Central Files
scope:
The Central Files of the Region VI office of the War Manpower Commission consist of correspondence, telegrams, reports, memorandums, meeting agenda and minutes, tables of statistical data, copies of state and regional office issuances, local office bulletins, organization charts, lists, and press releases.  The Region VI office, based in Chicago, attempted to rectify labor supply shortages and to stabilize workforce turnover in defense industries, agriculture, and transportation in Illinois, Indiana, and Wisconsin during the Second World War.

The records provide information about the development of workforce labor mobilization and employment stabilization policies and plans; occupational training; the designation of industries and services as essential to war production or locally needed; the temporary employment of foreign migrant workers; incidents and patterns of discrimination in hiring or employment because of race, color, gender, ethnic or national origin, or religion; the provision of adequate or affordable housing for war workers, including public housing, and incidents of prohibited discrimination in housing; and the relationship between War Manpower Commission staff and officials from other federal, state, and local government agencies.  The U.S. Employment Service, the Fair Employment Practice Committee, the War Production Board, the War Food Administration, the Selective Service System, and the railroad unemployment offices of the Railroad Retirement Board frequently operated in conjunction with the War Manpower Commission or under its direction.

The files include extensive documentation of a special survey by the Wage, Hour, and Public Contracts Division of the U.S. Department of Labor about compliance with the maximum number of full-time positions permitted for individual companies, violations of the employment "ceiling" numbers, and appeals by the companies.  A separate survey of the utilization of available persons for war-related work also is extensively documented.  

Other topics that are documented in the records include the manufacture of flame-throwers for use in the Pacific theater of war; the construction and opening of war workers housing by the Chicago Housing Authority at Bridgeport Homes, Lawndale Gardens, the Robert Brooks Homes, and the Frances Cabrini Green housing project in Chicago, Illinois; violations of War Manpower Commission regulations by companies and individual workers; the employment of white women and African-American men and women by companies engaged in the production of war materiel; and race discrimination.  Migrant workers from other regions of the United States, from Jamaica, Barbados, and the Bahamas in the Caribbean, and from Mexico under the Bracero Program are among the groups of temporary migrant workers who were placed in certain agricultural, transportation, and industrial jobs by the War Manpower Commission's Region VI office staff.

The files may include correspondence, notes, memoranda, copies of court documents, transcripts of testimony, exhibits, printed material, Federal Bureau of Investigation reports, telegrams, photographs, and news clippings.  

Some of the cases found in this series include bank cases and criminal cases on Indian Reservations. Others involved Indian land claims, civil rights, violations of the Selective Service Act from the Vietnam War era and earlier eras, Social Security Act, Revenue Act of 1941, Immigration Act, National Bankruptcy Act, Federal Reserve Act, Interstate Commerce Act, National Firearms Act, Commodity Credit Corporation, Government Communications System, Federal Escape Act, Soldiers and Sailors Civil Relief Act of 1940, prostitution prosecutions under the Mann Act, timber contracts on Indian Reservations, threats against the life of the President including President Reagan, income tax evasion, fraud against the U.S. Government, interstate transportation of stolen property, unlawful flight to avoid prosecutions, unauthorized entry and use of National Wildlife Refuge, mail fraud, theft of government property, and harboring or assisting a deserter.

title: Case Files
scope:
This series consists of records relating to criminal and civil investigations and prosecutions in Northern Ohio by the office of the United States Attorney for the Northern Judicial District of Ohio.  The files may include correspondence, notes, memoranda, copies of court documents, transcripts of testimony, exhibits, printed material, Federal Bureau of Investigation reports, telegrams, and news clippings.  

Some of the civil lawsuits and criminal prosecutions involved violations of the Safety Compliance Act, the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, the Food and Drug Act, the Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act, and the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.  The files relate to alleged acts of sabotage, mail fraud, evasion of draft registration, violations of federal interstate and foreign commerce laws, and patent infringement in Ohio.  Two prominent corporations, General Electric and General Motors, are numbered among the defendants in commerce-related investigations.  The National Guard shootings of students and deaths of four students during a May 4, 1970 protest against the Vietnam War at Kent State University are documented substantially in the U.S. Attorney investigation and prosecution files for a 1974 criminal trial in the U.S. District Court for the Northern (Cleveland) District of the Eastern Division of Ohio.

title: Case Files
scope:
This series consists of records compiled by the United States Attorney's staff during investigations and prosecutions of alleged criminal violations of federal law in eastern Michigan, including the Detroit area, or during civil lawsuits in which the United States Government or a federal agency was plaintiff or defendant.  The files commonly include correspondence; attorney notes; memoranda; telegrams; copies of court documents; transcripts of testimony; exhibits; printed materials; Federal Bureau of Investigation reports; investigative reports of the other federal agencies such as the Security and Exchange Commission, the Internal Revenue Service, or the Postal Inspector; transcripts of grand jury testimony; and news clippings.  Some investigations that are documented in the records were closed without pursuing indictments.

Some of the investigative cases arose from alleged violations of the McCarran Internal Security Act; the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938; the Sherman Anti-Trust Act; the Taft-Hartley Act and prohibited actions of labor union officials; and Alien Registration Act of 1940 (commonly called the Smith Act) and its prohibitions against Communist Party membership and subversive activities.  Other criminal investigations included alleged mail fraud, mortgage "milking" by real estate speculators in the Detroit vicinity during the 1960s, the failure to produce certain records before the United States House of Representatives' Committee on Un-American Activities, fraud against the U.S. Government, the cancellation of naturalization certificates for fraudulently denying membership in the Communist Party, interstate transportation of stolen property, income tax evasion, embezzlement of labor union funds, racketeering and interstate transportation in aid of racketeering, interstate transportation of wagering and gambling paraphernalia, the possession and interstate transportation of narcotics, failure to pay customs duties, and crime on the high seas and inland navigable waterways.  Some civil cases involve Federal Housing Administration foreclosures, U.S. Government divestiture under the provisions of the Clayton Act.  Notable cases and parties include William Frederick Koch and Koch Laboratories regarding the purported cancer treatment drug glyoxylide and its sale through the Christian Medical Research League; Sidney M. Bergman; American communist and Spanish Civil War veteran Saul Wellman; the Ford Motor Company; and the Wherry Housing Project for wartime defense workers.

title: The United States vs. Pietro Mecca and Paul Mennite

The letters written in Italian, as well as translated versions, are included in the case file. Mecca and Mennite were charged with violating postal laws. Mennite pled guilty and was sentenced to five years in the Leavenworth penitentiary. Mecca pled not guilty, but was found guilty and was also sent to five years in prison.

The United States of America vs John Trierweiler, James Elliot, Herbert Beasley, Ernest Poynter, Guy Morris, Martin Kiado, James Houston, Ed Garwood, Kenneth Bozarth, Erret Bozarth, Hubert Russell Tweedy, Charles Price, and Pearl Miller
scope:
This file consists of the 1943 criminal case file against John Trierweiler, James Elliot, Herbert Beasley, Ernest Poynter, Guy Morris, Martin Kiado, James Houston, Ed Garwood, Kenneth Bozarth, Erret Bozarth, Hubert Russell Tweedy, Charles Price, and Pearl Miller heard in the U.S. District Court in Danville, Illinois. Trierweiler was the Sheriff of Vigo County, Indiana and Elliot, Beasley, and Miller were Deputy Sheriffs and were acting as "State Officers" at the time. The defendants were indicted on violating the civil rights of Tennessee resident James Edward Person, specifically "the right and privilege not to be deprived of liberty and life without due process of law; the right to be secure in his person and to be immune from illegal arrest of assault and better; the right and privilege not to be denied the equal protection of the laws and the right and privilege not to be subject to different punishments, pains and penalties by reason of his race and color than are prescribed for the punishment of citizens."

According to the indictment, on October 12, 1942, Person, who was Black, "was a lawful traveler within the County of Vigo and the State of Indiana and was peaceably making his way from the County of Vigo toward and into the County of Edgar, Illinois; that James Edward Person had committed no offense against the laws of the State of Indiana or of the United States of America, and had not been charged with or convicted of any offense against the laws of the State of Indiana or the United States of America." The defendants "well knowing the premises aforesaid, then and there wantonly and recklessly circulated and passed from mouth to mouth, false suspicions, conjectures, and rumors concern the actions or alleged actions of said James Edward Person." The defendants then pursued Person through Vigo County, Indiana into Edgar County, Illinois where they shot and killed him. 

The case against the four State Officers Trierweiler, Elliot, Beasley, and Miller was dismissed (nolle prosequi). The remaining four defendants plead nolo contendere and paid a fine of $200 each.

title: United States of America vs. Theodore Donay
scope: This file is a treason case against Theodore Donay, a Detroit based German immigrant who aided escaped Nazi prisoner of war. Oberlieutant Hans Peter Krug, a Luftwaffe bomber pilot, was shot down over England on August 28th, 1940 and sent to a prison camp in Bowmanville, Ontario, Canada. Krug escaped on April 16, 1942 to Toronto, where he was stopped by military police, though they let him go. After making contact with a local priest, he procured a bus ticket to Windsor, across the river from Detroit. After crossing the Detroit River, Krug was put in contact with Max Stephan, a restaurant owner. Stephan, upon learning that is was Krug's birthday, took him out drinking and shopping, where they came into contact with another German, Theodore Donay. Stephan paid for Krug's bus to Chicago. Once in Chicago, Krug traveled to Columbus, Ohio, New York City and eventually made it to San Antonio, in hopes of crossing to Mexico to return to Germany to rejoin the German military.

The series includes letters received, copies of letters sent, forms, bills, receipts, and other documents created in the operation and administration of the agency. Some correspondents include Office of Indian Affairs; agency employees; business firms; and private individuals.
notes:
In 1858, an agency was established for the Chippewa of Lake Superior, who for 5 years had been under the Mackinac Agency. The new agency's correspondence was filed under "La Pointe," although it was not located at La Pointe and was known for several years as the Chippewa of Lake Superior Agency or the Lake Superior Agency.
By 1865, now known as the La Pointe Agency, although it operated from Superior, Wisconsin, from the Red Cliff Reservation, or from Bayfield, Wisconsin, opposite La Pointe. The Indians assigned to La Pointe were than living on several reservations in Wisconsin and Minnesota.
In 1927, the La Pointe Agency, the Laona Agency, the Red Cliff Agency, and the Mackinac Agency consolidated into the Lac du Flambeau Agency, effective  July 1, 1927.

Project Files Relating to Rivers and Harbors in Illinois and Northwest Indiana
scope:
The records consist of files about the construction, maintenance, and repair of locks, dams, levees, associated structures and machinery, and derrick boats, as well as the maintenance and improvement of harbors, rivers, and waterways.  The records consist of bids, contracts, site plans, technical drawings in blueprint and brownline media, architectural drawings of structures, detail drawings of machinery components, specification sheets, authorizations, cost estimates, surveys, progress and inspection reports, graphs, maps, and project-related letters.  A few files contain photographs and clippings of newspaper articles.  Files about the Illinois River, the Illinois Waterway, and tributaries relate to projects at lock and dam districts at LaGrange, Lockport, Joliet, Dresden Island, Marseilles, Starved Rock, Peoria, Pekin, Sangamon, Beardstown, Alton, Brandon Road, Hennepin, and other locales.

Some of the records also relate to wintertime ice floes on Illinois rivers, topographical studies, studies of the water table, stream gauge readings and charts, test reports of material and equipment, reports of dredging operations, and reports about encroachments upon waterways and obstructions that blocked navigation.  Files in the 812.3 and 812.4 file codes relate to topographic and ground water surveys in the vicinity of the Illinois Waterway, as well as "Riley Case" survey notes about the Kankakee River, with correspondence and copies of land descriptions.  Files in the 828.1 and 828.5 file codes relate to shipwrecks and wreckage that obstructed navigation in Calumet Harbor, the Grand Calumet River, the Chicago River, Chicago Harbor, the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, the Illinois Waterway, the Illinois River, Indiana Harbor, the Indiana Harbor Canal, Michigan City Harbor, and Waukegan Harbor, as well as wreck salvaging operations.
notes: The U.S. Engineering Office in Chicago, Illinois, became the Chicago District in 1880. The District was split into two Chicago Districts from 1901 to 1911, with the First Chicago District generally covering Lake Michigan projects and the Second Chicago District covering the Illinois Waterway connecting Chicago with the Mississippi River. In 1911, the two District re-combined to form a single Chicago District. The District was split again from 1929 to 1933, this time with the First District of Chicago covering the Illinois Waterway and the Second District of Chicago covering Lake Michigan projects. In both instances, when the two districts were merged in 1911 and 1933, the records of both the First and Second Districts were transferred to a new Chicago District.

scope: Valentine Goesaert and daughter Margaret Goesaert filed this 1947 suit against Owen J. Cleary, Felix H.H. Flynn and G. Mennen Williams, members of the Liquor Control Commission of Michigan concerning the April 30th, 1945 adoption of Act 133 of the Public Acts of the State of Michigan for 1945, Section 19(a) to the Liquor Law which allowed only men to own drinking establishments in cities with a population of 50,000. The Goesart's owned a bar in Dearborn, Michigan, that exceeded this number of residents. Women could only be licensed as bartenders if they were the wife or daughter of a male licensee. title: United States of America vs. Max Stephan
scope: This file is a treason case against Max Stephan, a Detroit based German immigrant who aided escaped Nazi prisoner of war. Oberlieutant Hans Peter Krug, a Luftwaffe bomber pilot, was shot down over England on August 28th, 1940 and sent to a prison camp in Bowmanville, Ontario, Canada. Krug escaped on April 16, 1942 to Toronto, where he was stopped by military police, though they let him go. After making contact with a local priest, he procured a bus ticket to Windsor, across the river from Detroit. After crossing the Detroit River, Krug was put in contact with Max Stephan, a restaurant owner. Stephan, upon learning that is was Krug'd birthday, took him out drinking and shopping, where they came into contact with another German, Theodore Donay. Stephan paid for Krug's bus to Chicago. Once in Chicago, Krug traveled to Columbus, Ohio, New York City and eventually made it to San Antonio, in hopes of crossing to Mexico to return to Germany to rejoin the German military.
notes: See related case "United States of America vs. Theodore Donay" (National Archives Identifier 485326917).

In her Petition for Habeas Corpus, she protested the deportation warrant issued due to her spoken agreement with Government officials that her alien status would be forgiven by informing on Dillinger. notes: Historically, she is known as the Woman in Red due to the color of the clothing she wore when was with Dillinger the night he was gunned down, though she is said to have worn orange.

title: Law Record Books
scope: This series contain complete records of law cases herd by the U.S. Circuit Court located in Indianapolis, which heard cases primarily from central and southern Indiana.  The date of the court term and the case title are entered for each case.  Examples of procedural entries are complete copies of the complaint, defendant's reply, motions, depositions, court rulings and judgment; in some instances, exhibits and testimony were transcribed.  Volumes 18-20, 1862-1865, contain in addition to law cases, several cases of a criminal nature, many of which resulted from wartime activities such as violations of the draft law, harboring deserters, and charges of conspiracy and treason.  Among these is the famous Ex parte Milligan case which ultimately involved the U.S. Supreme Court and a ruling on the executive power of a President during wartime.
